payload.body: Contact quotient (Cn) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the fraction of the fundamental period T0 during which the vocal folds are in contact in voiced phonation. From the electroglottographic signal (EGG) or glottal-flow waveform g(n), the contact phase is the interval during which the signal indicates vocal fold contact, and Cn = contact phase / T0. Parameters: (1) the electroglottographic or glottal-flow signal estimated per voiced frame, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the contact-phase extraction method (EGG derivative zero crossings or glottal-flow extrema). It is reported as a dimensionless ratio; the maintained reference range for typical phonation sits near 0.5-0.7, and an elevated contact quotient indicates prolonged vocal fold contact as in pressed or hypofunctional phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software (Praat, laryngology suites) from the glottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. [formal: quotientia contactus | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.body: Period perturbation is a class of voice-quality parameters that quantify the cycle-to-cycle variation in the fundamental period of voiced speech. The general measure computes the normalized difference between consecutive periods: given N consecutive glottal cycles with periods P_i, perturbation = normalized deviation of |P_{i+1} - P_i| relative to the mean period. Named variants include: APQ1 (average absolute difference quotient), JRR (jitter ratio), and JDP (jitter absolute difference). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal, (2) the pitch-synchronous segmentation at cycle boundaries, (3) the specific perturbation variant formula. Reported in percent or absolute units (ms). Persistence mechanism: maintained as a measurement class by the discipline of laryngology and speech science; implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Praat, laryngology suites), taught in voice-disorder curricula, and standardized in clinical practice. [formal: perturbatio periodica | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Period perturbation is a class of voice-quality parameters that quantify the cycle-to-cycle variation in the fundamental period of voiced speech. The general measure computes the normalized difference between consecutive periods: given N consecutive glottal cycles with periods P_i, perturbation = normalized deviation of |P_{i+1} - P_i| relative to the mean period. Named variants include: APQ1 (average absolute difference quotient), JRR (jitter ratio), and JDP (jitter absolute difference). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal, (2) the pitch-synchronous segmentation at cycle boundaries, (3) the specific perturbation variant formula. Reported in percent or absolute units (ms). Persistence mechanism: maintained as a measurement class by the discipline of laryngology and speech science; implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Praat, laryngology suites), taught in voice-disorder curricula, and standardized in clinical practice. payload.body: Amplitude perturbation is a class of voice-quality parameters that quantify the cycle-to-cycle variation in the amplitude (energy level) of voiced speech. The general measure computes the normalized difference between consecutive cycle amplitudes: given N consecutive glottal cycles with amplitudes A_i, perturbation = normalized deviation of |A_{i+1} - A_i| relative to the mean amplitude. Named variants include: APQ3 (average absolute difference quotient over 3-cycle windows) and the standard deviation variant (standard deviation of cycle amplitudes divided by their mean). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal, (2) the pitch-synchronous segmentation at cycle boundaries, (3) the specific perturbation variant formula. Reported in percent or decibels (20*log10(std/mean)). Persistence mechanism: maintained as a measurement class by the discipline of laryngology and speech science; implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Praat, laryngology suites), taught in voice-disorder curricula, and standardized in clinical practice. [formal: perturbatio amplitude | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.name: excitation-signal
payload.scope: A human-made signal processing construct — the residual waveform obtained by removing a known or estimated system transfer function from an observed signal, yielding the estimated input that drove the system. payload.body: Excitation signal is the residual waveform obtained by applying inverse filtering to an observed signal x(n) through an estimated transfer function H(z), yielding the estimated input e(n) = x(n) * H_inv(z) where H_inv(z) = 1/H(z). In speech processing, H(z) is the vocal-tract linear-prediction filter and e(n) is the glottal-flow waveform; in general DSP, e(n) is the recovered source signal that excited the system. Parameters: (1) the input signal x(n) — the observed output of the system, (2) the transfer function H(z) to remove — typically a linear-prediction all-pole model or measured frequency response, (3) the inverse filter H_inv(z) — the reciprocal of H(z), implemented as an all-pole filter. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic implementation in DSP software (Praat, MATLAB, Kaldi), documentation in signal processing literature, and standardized use in source-filter separation, speech analysis, and acoustic modeling. [formal: excitatio-signalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.name: residual-signal
payload.scope: A human-made signal processing construct — a time-series of differences between an observed signal and its model-based reconstruction. Distinct from statistical residuals (scalar differences in regression), residual-signal is a waveform: the per-sample error between the observed signal and the output of a model system driven by the same input. In speech analysis, the residual-signal is the excitation signal obtained by inverse-filtering the speech signal through the estimated vocal-tract filter; in other domains, it is the model error waveform that reveals what the model fails to explain.

payload.body: Residual signal is the per-sample difference signal r(n) = x(n) - x_hat(n), where x(n) is the observed signal and x_hat(n) is the reconstructed signal produced by a model system. The residual-signal captures what the model fails to account for: in speech processing, it is the glottal excitation waveform after removing the vocal-tract filter; in system identification, it is the model-error waveform that reveals unmodeled dynamics or noise. Computed by: (1) obtaining the model (e.g., an all-pole linear-prediction filter), (2) filtering the input to produce the model output, (3) subtracting the model output from the observed signal. Parameters: (1) the observed signal x(n), (2) the model structure and parameters, (3) the subtraction method. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic implementation in DSP software (Praat, MATLAB, Kaldi), documentation in signal processing literature, and standardized use in model evaluation, speech analysis, and adaptive filtering. payload.name: source-filter-separation
payload.scope: A human-made signal processing technique for decomposing an observed signal into its source (excitation) and filter (resonance) components. The technique separates what generates energy from what shapes it.

payload.body: source-filter-separation is a human-made signal processing technique that decomposes an observed signal into two additive or convolutive components: a source (excitation) component representing the energy origin, and a filter (resonance) component representing the shaping mechanism. The technique operates by applying one of several decomposition methods — (1) inverse filtering, where the estimated transfer function H(z) is inverted to recover e(n) = x(n) * H_inv(z), (2) deconvolution, where the source is recovered by frequency-domain division of the spectrum by the filter spectrum, or (3) cepstral analysis, where the logarithm of the spectrum separates slowly-varying filter envelope from rapidly-varying source structure. Parameters: (1) the input signal x(n), (2) the source-filter model assumptions (convolutive vs additive), (3) the decomposition method and its parameters. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic implementation in DSP software (Praat, MATLAB, Kaldi), documentation in signal processing textbooks (Rabiner and Schafer, Oppenheim and Schafer), and standardized use in speech analysis, audio processing, and system identification pipelines. [formal: separatio fontis-filtrum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: The asymmetry coefficient is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the asymmetry of the glottal airflow pulse in voiced phonation. It measures the degree to which the glottal flow pulse is skewed toward the open or close phase of the glottal cycle. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0, the asymmetry coefficient is computed as the ratio of the open-phase duration to the close-phase duration within the period, or equivalently as the skewness of the flow pulse. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform estimated per voiced frame, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the asymmetry computation method (open-phase/close-phase ratio or flow-pulse skewness). It is reported as a dimensionless ratio; a value of 1 indicates symmetric phonation, while values deviating from 1 indicate pressed (value above 1) or breathy (value below 1) phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software from the glottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. [formal: coefficient asymmetricus | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.body: The return phase is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the return phase of the glottal airflow pulse in voiced phonation. It measures the timing of the return of the glottal flow to its baseline after the excitation pulse, characterizing the decay characteristics of the glottal source. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0, the return phase is computed as the time from the flow maximum to the return of the flow to baseline within the period. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform estimated per voiced frame, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the return-phase extraction method (time from flow maximum to baseline return). It is reported in milliseconds or as a fraction of the fundamental period; the maintained reference range for typical phonation is within the normal glottal cycle timing, and deviations indicate glottal source abnormalities such as pressed or breathy phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software from the glottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. [formal: phase reditus | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.body: The glottogram (glottal-flow waveform) is a human-made time-series representation of estimated glottal airflow obtained by inverse filtering the speech signal. The speech signal x(n) is processed with the inverse of the estimated vocal-tract transfer function — the inverse linear-prediction filter 1/(1 - Σ_k a_k z^-k) over voiced frames — yielding the glottal-flow sequence g(n). Parameters: (1) the speech signal x(n) frame-aligned to voicing, (2) the vocal-tract filter estimate as linear-prediction coefficients a_k with prediction order p, (3) the frame and windowing parameters of the inverse filter. The glottogram encodes the excitation of the source-filter model: its derivatives (contact quotient, open quotient, return phase, asymmetry coefficient) constitute the voice-quality measurement family. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech analysis toolkits (Praat, MATLAB, Kaldi), documented in speech science textbooks, and used clinically to estimate glottal flow for voice-disorder analysis; persists as per-frame estimated flow values and their derived parameters. [formal: glottalis fluxus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.name: voice-onset-time
payload.scope: A human-made voice-quality measurement parameter quantifying the temporal offset between glottal-source onset and acoustic voice onset in the first phonation cycle, built to persist as a standardized clinical parameter in speech science and laryngology that classifies breathy, modal, and creaky phonation.

payload.body: Voice onset time (VOT) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the temporal offset between the onset of the glottal source and the onset of acoustic voice in the first phonation cycle, typically measured after a voiceless context such as a plosive. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the acoustic waveform x(n), VOT is computed as the interval from the first flow maximum (first glottal closure, the glottal-source onset) to the first reliable periodic component of the acoustic signal (acoustic voice onset), reported in milliseconds. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform estimated per voiced frame (the glottogram), (2) the acoustic waveform with the first phonation cycle, (3) the onset-detection criterion for each endpoint (first flow maximum from the glottogram; periodicity onset by autocorrelation or waveform marking). It is reported in milliseconds; the maintained reference ranges separate phonation types — long (positive) VOT when acoustic onset leads glottal closure, breathy phonation; near-zero (short) VOT when the two onsets are simultaneous, modal phonation; negative VOT when glottal closure precedes acoustic onset, creaky phonation — and deviations mark glottal-source abnormalities. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software from the glottogram and acoustic waveform, taught in voice-disorder curricula and speech-language pathology, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. [formal: tempus initii vocis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.name: electroglottogram
payload.scope: A human-made per-frame time-series waveform of glottal vocal-fold contact, produced by demodulating the electroglottographic voltage signal; it tracks the open/close cycle of the glottis and serves as the measured counterpart of the glottal-source model in clinical laryngology and voice-disorder assessment.

payload.name: electroglottogram

payload.body: The electroglottogram is the demodulated envelope of the electroglottographic (EGG) voltage waveform. EGG passes a small alternating current through the vocal folds and records the voltage across them; because glottal contact area modulates vocal-fold impedance — high impedance when the glottis is open, low impedance when the folds are in contact — the peak-to-peak voltage amplitude is inversely proportional to glottal contact area. Demodulating the per-cycle peak-to-peak voltage produces a continuous time series whose amplitude is inversely proportional to glottal contact area, tracking the open/close cycle of the glottis. Parameters: (1) the excitation current — a small AC current kept below the safety threshold (typically ~0.5 mA peak at ~2.5 kHz); (2) electrode placement — two submental/neck electrodes completing the current path through the larynx; (3) demodulation — per-cycle peak-to-peak voltage measurement producing a continuous signal. The electroglottogram persists as a measured time series of glottal contact in clinical laryngology and voice-disorder assessment (e.g., Kay PENTAGRAM, the laryngograph). [formal: electroglottogramma | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.scope: A human-made measurement construct of the periodic open/close cycle of the glottis during voiced phonation, comprising the opening, closed, and transition phases, built to persist as the foundational phenomenon underlying glottal airflow and vocal-fold contact in speech science and clinical laryngology.

payload.body: The glottal cycle is the periodic open/close cycle of the glottis during voiced phonation, comprising the opening phase (glottal opening from closed to open), the closed phase (vocal folds in contact), and the transition phases (closing and opening). It is measured per pitch period from the glottal-flow waveform or the electroglottogram envelope. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0, the glottal cycle is partitioned into phases: opening (from the flow maximum to the minimum), closed (the flow at or near zero), and closing (from the minimum back to the maximum). Its parameters include the open quotient (ratio of open-phase duration to the period), the contact quotient (from the electroglottogram envelope), the asymmetry coefficient (ratio of open-phase to close-phase duration), and the return phase (time from flow maximum to return to baseline). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software from the glottogram and electroglottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. [formal: cyclus glottis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.name: glottal-pulse
payload.scope: A human-made measurement construct of the periodic airflow excitation pulse generated by vocal fold vibration during voiced phonation, built to persist as the source phenomenon underlying glottal airflow and vocal-fold contact in speech science and clinical laryngology.

payload.body: The glottal pulse is the periodic excitation of airflow generated by vocal fold vibration during voiced phonation. It is the source excitation that, when filtered by the vocal-tract transfer function, produces the speech signal. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, the glottal pulse is identified per pitch period as the airflow excursion whose onset coincides with the glottal opening and whose decay returns the flow to baseline. Parameters: (1) the vocal fold vibration cycle generating the airflow pulse, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the pulse shape parameters — rise time, duration, and amplitude of the airflow excursion. It persists as a standardized source-excitation construct in speech science, implemented in voice-analysis and synthesis toolkits, taught in speech production curricula, and used to model the glottal source in source-filter separation. [formal: pulsus glottidis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.name: glottal-to-noise-ratio
payload.scope: A human-made voice-quality parameter quantifying the ratio of harmonic (voiced) energy to noise energy in a speech signal, built to persist as a standardized clinical measure of phonation type and voice-disorder assessment in laryngology and speech-language pathology.

payload.name: glottal-to-noise-ratio

payload.body: The glottal-to-noise ratio (HNR) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the balance between the periodic (harmonic) component and the aperiodic (noise) component of a speech signal, reported in decibels as 10 log10(E_harmonic / E_noise). Given a voiced segment of the speech signal and a fundamental-frequency estimate, the harmonic energy is measured over the frequency bands at the fundamental and its integer harmonics, and the noise energy over the inter-harmonic regions, so that a high ratio indicates a dominantly periodic (modal) source and a low ratio indicates an aperiodic (breathy, harsh, or dysphonic) source. Parameters: (1) the analyzed voiced segment, (2) the fundamental-frequency estimate f0 locating the harmonic comb, (3) the number of harmonics covered and the band-widths around each harmonic, (4) the energy or power measure per band. It is reported in decibels with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical parameter implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Praat, laryngology suites), documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained as a member of the voice-quality measurement map. [formal: ratio glottalis ad sonum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]
